title: View-Disagreement Escalation for Robust Web-Agent Trajectory Judges

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to detect unreliable LLM-judge predictions on web-agent trajectories arising from manipulated chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Paper [1] explicitly addresses the brittleness of LLM judges when CoT reasoning traces are manipulated, showing that such manipulation undermines agent evaluation reliability. This aligns with the same problem-class objective of detecting unreliable LLM judgments caused by CoT manipulation.

### Mechanism
The mechanism is a training-free two-stage framework comparing judgments from two counterfactual input views (with CoT vs without CoT) and selectively escalating disagreement cases to strict evidence-anchored evaluation. Paper [15] introduces a counterfactual evaluation framework for detecting blind attacks in LLM-based systems, which involves re-evaluating submissions against deliberately false ground-truth answers to detect discrepancies. While the specific implementation differs, the underlying primitive of counterfactual comparison to detect reliability issues is substantively equivalent. Additionally, paper [14] proposes selective escalation based on confidence assessment to ensure reliable evaluation, which matches the escalation primitive in the mechanism.

### Evaluation
The contribution evaluates its framework on AgentRewardBench, where escalation on view disagreement yields a 63% relative reduction in attack sensitivity while maintaining competitive F1. Paper [6] introduces FaithCoT-Bench, a benchmark for instance-level faithfulness of CoT reasoning, which is a named benchmark family for evaluating CoT reliability. Although the specific benchmark instance differs, the evaluation design of using a benchmark to assess CoT reliability is covered. Paper [14] also uses selective evaluation frameworks to validate reliability improvements, aligning with the selective escalation evaluation design.

### Domain
The domain is LLM-as-a-judge applied to web agent evaluation. Paper [9] surveys the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm broadly, covering its application across diverse fields, including agent evaluation. Paper [3] extends LLM-as-a-judge to agentic systems, explicitly addressing web-agent evaluation. Both papers establish that the domain of LLM-as-a-judge for web-agent evaluation is covered.

However, the *purpose* here is specifically to *detect* unreliable predictions caused by CoT manipulation — a defensive/detection goal. Paper [1] introduces the *attack* (showing the vulnerability exists) but does not pursue the purpose of detecting or defending against it. Paper [22] evaluates robustness but focuses on meta-evaluation rather than a detection mechanism for manipulated CoT. Paper [14] ("Trust or Escalate") proposes selective evaluation to detect when to trust LLM judge outputs, which is close but targets general confidence/human agreement rather than CoT manipulation specifically. Paper [6] ("FaithCoT-Bench") addresses "deciding whether a specific CoT is faithful," which is substantively equivalent to detecting unreliable predictions arising from unfaithful CoT. The purpose of [6] — instance-level faithfulness detection of CoT — is the same problem class as detecting unreliable judge predictions from manipulated CoT.

Paper [6] states: "they leave open the practical challenge of deciding whether a specific CoT is faithful" — this is the same objective at the problem-class level.

---

**MECHANISM: Training-free two-stage framework comparing judgments from two counterfactual input views (with CoT vs without CoT) and selectively escalating disagreement cases to strict evidence-anchored evaluation.**

The core primitive is: (1) generate two views by including vs. excluding CoT, (2) compare outputs, (3) escalate disagreements. 

Paper [15] ("Counterfactual Evaluation for Blind Attack Detection") proposes augmenting standard evaluation with counterfactual evaluation and detecting attacks when the system validates an answer under both real and false ground-truth — a two-view comparison framework for detecting manipulation. The primitive of "compare judgments under two counterfactual input conditions; flag disagreement as suspicious" is substantively equivalent.

Paper [14] ("Trust or Escalate") introduces selective escalation: "assess the confidence of judge models and selectively decide when to trust its judgement" with escalation to human review on low-confidence cases. This covers the escalation component.

Paper [11] ("CoT Unfaithfulness as Disguised Accuracy") uses the with-CoT vs. without-CoT comparison as a measure of CoT dependence/faithfulness — the same counterfactual view comparison primitive.

Combining [15] (counterfactual two-view comparison for attack detection) and [14] (selective escalation on disagreement) covers the full mechanism. Paper [15] is the closest single match for the combined primitive.

**EVALUATION: Evaluated on AgentRewardBench, with escalation on view disagreement yielding 63% relative reduction in attack sensitivity while maintaining competitive F1.**

AgentRewardBench is a specific named benchmark. Paper [1] ("Gaming the Judge") introduces the attack framework evaluated on agent trajectories and uses attack success rate / F1-type metrics for LLM judge evaluation. Paper [22] uses robustness evaluation of LLM judges with attack sensitivity metrics. The evaluation design — measuring attack sensitivity reduction and F1 on an agent-evaluation benchmark — follows the same design as [1] and [22]: LLM-judge robustness evaluation with attack success rate and accuracy/F1 metrics. AgentRewardBench is a specific benchmark instance; the design (judge robustness under attack, F1/accuracy metrics) is covered by [1] and [22].

Paper [1] operates directly in LLM-as-a-judge for agent evaluation. Paper [3] ("Agent-as-a-Judge") also works in agent evaluation. Paper [9] ("Survey on LLM-as-a-Judge") covers the LLM-as-a-judge domain broadly. This domain is clearly covered.
